summary: This document provides a security framework for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). It covers the security aspects specific to MPLS-TP, which extends MPLS with new OAM capabilities, transport-style path protection, and heavy reliance on static provisioning. It describes potential threats and mitigations.

subtitle: Security framework for MPLS Transport Profile networks

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) networks introduce new security challenges with their emphasis on static provisioning, in-band OAM, and transport-oriented protection mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: This framework identifies specific security threats to MPLS-TP systems and describes defensive techniques including authentication, access control, and infrastructure isolation.
tldr.outcome: The framework provides guidance for operators and vendors to assess and protect MPLS-TP deployments against threats like label manipulation, denial of service attacks, and compromised network management systems.

today: RFC 6941 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a reference for operators implementing MPLS-TP networks and security architects designing carrier transport infrastructure.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is an extension of MPLS technology designed for carrier transport networks. It adds new capabilities for operations, administration and maintenance (OAM), includes transport-oriented path protection, and relies heavily on static provisioning through Network Management Systems (NMSs) and Operational Support Systems (OSSs).

This framework extends RFC 5920, which covers security for MPLS and GMPLS networks generally. It focuses specifically on security aspects unique to MPLS-TP, including threats that arise from its distinctive architecture and operational model. The document describes potential security threats and mitigation procedures for MPLS-TP networks and their interconnections with other MPLS and GMPLS networks.
sections.eli5: MPLS-TP is a way to move data through networks that phone companies use. This document explains what bad things could happen and how to stop them.

sections.title: Security Models
sections.content:
The framework defines two primary security reference models based on the placement of Service Provider (SP) boundaries. A trusted zone is defined as the part of the network where a single SP has total operational control.

In Reference Model 1, a single SP controls the entire path from one Provider Edge (PE) or Terminating Provider Edge (T-PE) device to another. This applies to Single-Segment Pseudowire (SS-PW) connections and Multi-Segment Pseudowire (MS-PW) topologies where the entire path is within one SP's control. Security boundaries clearly separate trusted zones from untrusted external networks.

In Reference Model 2, a single SP does not have end-to-end control. Switching Provider Edge (S-PE) or T-PE devices may be controlled by different SPs, customers, or partners. This creates multiple trusted zones with untrusted boundaries between them, introducing inter-provider security concerns. Security boundaries must be carefully analyzed for each individual network topology.
sections.eli5: There are two main ways to set up a network: one company controls everything, or different companies control different parts. Each setup has different ways bad guys might attack.

sections.title: Security Threats
sections.content:
MPLS-TP networks face distinct security threats that differ from traditional MPLS. Attacks on the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) and the G-ACh Label (GAL) include label manipulation: insertion of false labels, modification, deletion, or replay of OAM messages. These attacks can cause unauthorized protection switchover, inability to restore Label Switched Paths (LSPs), or loss of network connectivity.

Denial of Service (DoS) attacks are a particular concern in MPLS-TP. Attackers can generate excessive G-ACh/GAL and Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) messages that consume significant bandwidth and cause congestion. Because MPLS-TP uses in-band OAM (OAM messages share the same data path as user traffic), such attacks have direct operational impact.

Management system attacks are especially critical in MPLS-TP deployments due to their heavy reliance on static provisioning. Attacks on the NMS can originate from external attackers (outside the trusted zone) or insider threats (from within the trusted zone with authorized access). Compromised communication channels between NMS and network devices, or unauthorized access to provisioning tools, can enable disclosure of information, generation of false OAM messages, LSP takedown, misdirection to wrong tunnel endpoints, and DoS attacks.
sections.eli5: Bad guys can trick the network by sending fake messages that look real, flood it with too much traffic, or hack the management system that controls everything.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
sections.content:
Authentication is the primary defense mechanism for mitigating MPLS-TP security threats. This includes entity authentication for identity verification, management system authentication, peer-to-peer authentication, and message integrity checks with replay detection. Network-based access controls such as packet filtering and firewalls, combined with host-based access controls and isolation techniques, form multiple layers of defense.

For protecting the MPLS-TP infrastructure itself, isolated infrastructure using dedicated network resources can reduce attack surface. In multi-provider scenarios, using non-IP-based communication paths for trusted zones makes them unreachable from external networks via IP.

Particularly important for NMS security are entity authentication for identity verification, encryption for confidentiality, message integrity and replay detection, and user access control with event logging. These must be applied comprehensively to NMSs and provisioning applications due to the critical role of static provisioning in MPLS-TP operations.

Verification of connectivity mechanisms can protect against deliberate or accidental misconnection by tracing routes of LSPs in both control and data planes, enabling end-to-end and segment-by-segment resource verification.
sections.eli5: Defend the network by making sure only real messages get through, using secret codes to check identities, logging everything that happens, and keeping the management system separate and protected.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
The security techniques described apply to MPLS-TP in ways that depend on the specific operational environment. The document emphasizes that techniques are not requirements for all MPLS-TP deployments; rather, protocol designers should provide a full set of security capabilities that can be selected appropriately.

MPLS-TP providers must determine which techniques apply to their specific service offerings and customer requirements. End users should assess the value of these techniques to their service needs. The choice of security mechanisms depends on factors like the trust model between providers, the criticality of services carried, the threats present in the deployment environment, and the operational expertise available.

The defensive techniques presented here use mature, widely implemented technologies that are practical to deploy. Effective security requires careful planning at the design stage, with clear definition of trust boundaries and security policies for each network topology.
sections.eli5: Different networks need different levels of protection depending on what they do and who they trust. Pick the right tools for your situation and set them up carefully.
